notes.title: Choose the correct model and architecture
notes.symptom: A driver or repair package says it is incompatible, or the device model is uncertain.
notes.firstAction: Open Settings > System > About and record the system type and Windows version.
steps: Run msinfo32 and read System Manufacturer, System Model and System Type; use the actual machine rather than a similar-looking product name.
Match the package to that model, Windows version and processor architecture. An x64 application running under emulation does not make an x64 hardware driver suitable for an ARM device.
Keep the model/build record in the private ticket and choose the matching manufacturer download before retrying.
notes.expected: The selected package explicitly supports the actual model and architecture and opens without the compatibility error.
notes.ifUnresolved: If no supported driver exists, use a supported class-driver/device path or escalate compatibility; do not force an unrelated INF.

notes.title: Find the background program blocking an app
notes.symptom: An application fails in normal startup but works when optional background software is absent.
notes.firstAction: Record the exact reproduction and the currently enabled startup items before changing them.
steps: Use Microsoft’s clean-boot procedure in an agreed service window: hide Microsoft services and identify the optional services/startup items under test. Coordinate any managed security or remote-access dependency.
Retest the same application. If the failure disappears, re-enable a recorded subset at a time and restart to narrow the conflict.
Restore the normal configuration after the test; repair or update the identified conflicting product instead of leaving unrelated services disabled.
notes.expected: A specific enabled item reproducibly changes the result, and normal startup is restored with the resolved configuration.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the same failure persists in the controlled startup state, stop disabling more software and move to the application’s own diagnostic route.

notes.title: Correct a bad clock before chasing sign-in errors
notes.symptom: Several secure sites or sign-ins fail and the displayed date or time is wrong.
notes.firstAction: Compare the device’s date, time and time zone with a trusted current reference.
steps: Open Settings > Time & language > Date & time and distinguish an incorrect time zone from an incorrect clock.
On a managed domain PC, read w32tm /query /status to identify the existing synchronization source; restore the organization’s time path rather than choosing an arbitrary public server.
On an unmanaged PC, correct the supported automatic-time settings, synchronize, then reopen the affected sign-in or site.
notes.expected: The clock stays correct and the original authentication or certificate-date failure no longer occurs.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the clock resets after power loss, investigate firmware time/battery or management policy; do not bypass certificate warnings.

notes.title: Stop website notification popups
notes.symptom: Desktop alerts claim the PC is infected, but the alerts identify a browser or website sender.
notes.firstAction: Record the sender and close the alert without opening its link.
steps: In Microsoft Edge open Settings > Privacy, search, and services > Site permissions > All sites; choose the unwanted site and select See more.
Set that site’s Notifications permission to Block; inspect related extensions and recent downloads if the alerts began with an installation.
Retest with the browser restarted. Use the malware route if executable detections, persistence or other compromise evidence remains.
notes.expected: The unwanted site can no longer send notifications and normal browsing still works.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the sender is not the browser, or alerts persist after permission removal, identify the actual installed application before removing anything.

notes.title: Undo an accidental allowed-threat decision
notes.symptom: A known detection was allowed earlier and the same item remains present.
notes.firstAction: Open Windows Security > Virus & threat protection and review the exact detection and its earlier disposition.
steps: With the authorized administrator available, check Protection history and Allowed threats for the matching item; distinguish an allowed action from quarantine or a failed remediation.
For a confirmed accidental allowance, choose the supported Don’t allow action, update the active protection and rescan the affected scope.
Record the new disposition and whether the file or startup entry returns after restart.
notes.expected: The unintended allowance is removed and the confirmed threat has a recorded remediation result.
notes.ifUnresolved: If policy controls the setting or the detection recurs, involve the managed protection owner and investigate the entry point rather than adding exclusions.

notes.title: Find why the offline scan never runs
notes.symptom: The offline-scan request returns to Windows without a documented completed scan.
notes.firstAction: Check the device platform and the Microsoft Defender Offline prerequisites before requesting another restart.
steps: Confirm the supported Windows edition/architecture, the required primary antivirus state and availability of the BitLocker recovery key.
Run reagentc /info from an elevated local Windows session to inspect recovery-environment status; do not publish recovery configuration or credentials.
Resolve the documented prerequisite with the device owner, then request the offline scan through Windows Security and review the resulting protection history.
notes.expected: The offline environment actually runs and a result can be tied to that scan attempt.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not treat an ordinary reboot as a clean scan. Unsupported platforms or a broken recovery environment need the appropriate supported recovery route.

notes.title: Protect backups before testing a restore
notes.symptom: Compromised machines can still reach the backup destination or its administration account.
notes.firstAction: Have the incident lead separate backup access from the affected systems using a known-clean administration path.
steps: Identify offline, immutable or otherwise isolated recovery copies and record their dates without attaching them to an affected endpoint.
Check whether the backup account or repository was modified during the incident; preserve access logs and the incident timeline.
Restore a selected pre-incident sample into an isolated clean environment and test the actual data before planning production recovery.
notes.expected: A usable recovery point is demonstrated and remains outside the attacker’s current access path.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the backup system or administrative identity is also compromised, involve the incident and backup owners before changing retention or deleting snapshots.

notes.title: Contain stolen account access as well as the PC
notes.symptom: The incident involves privileged credentials, suspicious sessions or activity on more than one device.
notes.firstAction: Use a known-clean device and have the identity administrator identify the affected account and scope.
steps: Preserve relevant sign-in and audit evidence before applying the organization’s account containment procedure.
Use the supported identity response to block or secure the account, reset credentials and revoke applicable sessions; review unauthorized authentication methods and app access.
Recheck access and sign-in activity from a clean session while endpoint containment continues.
notes.expected: The account has an evidenced containment state and unauthorized access paths are addressed separately from endpoint rebuilding.
notes.ifUnresolved: A password change alone is not a complete incident release. Escalate if administrators, federation or multiple identities are affected.

notes.title: Evaluate a decryptor without risking the evidence
notes.symptom: A supposed decryptor is offered for the observed ransomware family.
notes.firstAction: Preserve the ransom note and encrypted originals, and check the family against the official No More Ransom resources.
steps: Use only the matched vendor/project instructions; a similar ransom-note name is not proof that a decryptor supports the exact variant.
In a known-clean, isolated recovery environment, prepare separate copies of representative encrypted files and any required original/encrypted pairs.
Test the supported decryptor on those copies and open recovered files in their real applications before considering wider use.
notes.expected: The test demonstrates usable files for the exact supported variant while original evidence remains intact.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the variant is unsupported, files remain corrupt or a website asks for unapproved payment/credentials, stop and continue the incident-led restore plan.

notes.title: Separate useful cache from memory pressure
notes.symptom: A PC shows high memory use and someone proposes a RAM-cleaning utility.
notes.firstAction: Reproduce the slowdown while watching Task Manager > Performance > Memory.
steps: Compare available memory and committed memory with the workload; use RAMMap to distinguish active usage from standby/file-cache pages.
Close one agreed nonessential application and repeat the same task, keeping the before/after observations.
If one process grows repeatedly without releasing memory, collect its identity and reproduction for the application owner rather than routinely emptying caches.
notes.expected: The evidence identifies actual workload pressure or a growing process, rather than treating every cached page as lost RAM.
notes.ifUnresolved: If memory pressure does not correlate with the delay, return to CPU, storage and network evidence.

notes.title: Find the optional app delaying sign-in
notes.symptom: The desktop appears quickly but the user must wait before starting normal work.
notes.firstAction: Time the same sign-in-to-ready task before making changes.
steps: Open Task Manager > Startup apps and record enabled entries and their reported impact.
Disable one agreed optional item, keeping required security, accessibility and managed-support software in place, then repeat the same restart/sign-in test.
Keep only the evidenced change, and re-enable entries that did not improve the measured task.
notes.expected: The user’s real ready-to-work time improves and required background functions still run.
notes.ifUnresolved: If delays occur before sign-in or persist with the candidate disabled, investigate boot, domain, storage or profile dependencies.

notes.title: Find what an app is waiting for
notes.symptom: One application freezes while disk or network-file activity continues.
notes.firstAction: Check storage health before recording a short trace on healthy storage.
steps: In Process Monitor, filter to the affected process and reproduce the pause once; stop capture immediately afterward.
Compare the pause time with repeated file, registry or network-path operations and their durations; a single ACCESS DENIED or NAME NOT FOUND is not automatically the cause.
Test the specific blocked path or dependency, then repeat the same application action with the scoped correction.
notes.expected: A particular wait or repeated failing operation correlates with the freeze and the corrected task is measurably better.
notes.ifUnresolved: Escalate an unresolved trace to the application owner with a private, bounded capture; stop tracing if the disk becomes unstable.

notes.title: Explain a laptop that slows down on battery
notes.symptom: The same application is responsive on AC power but slow when unplugged.
notes.firstAction: Repeat a short, identical workload on the approved charger and on battery.
steps: Inspect Settings > System > Power & battery for the active power mode and energy-saving state.
Check whether the charger is recognized and suitable for the model; record any low-power or charging warning.
Choose an approved power mode for the workload and retest without disabling thermal or battery protections.
notes.expected: The performance difference is tied to an observed power state, charger issue or policy rather than an unexplained cleanup change.
notes.ifUnresolved: If performance drops while hot or on a correctly rated charger, investigate cooling, battery condition or firmware using the exact OEM guidance.

notes.title: Resolve a missing DISM repair source
notes.symptom: DISM reports that source files could not be found, including a source-related servicing error.
notes.firstAction: Record the exact servicing error, installed Windows build, architecture and language.
steps: Check whether Windows Update can supply repair content under the device’s policy before selecting a local source.
Use Microsoft’s repair-source guidance to match the installed image and required language/servicing level; identify the correct image index when the source contains several editions.
Retry only the documented repair against the confirmed running installation or explicitly identified offline image, then retain its final result.
notes.expected: DISM accepts the compatible source and finishes, or returns a narrower actionable error.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not substitute random DLLs or use an unrelated ISO. Recurring corruption with I/O faults belongs to storage recovery.

notes.title: Identify what SFC could not repair
notes.symptom: System File Checker reports unresolved corruption after the documented component-store sequence.
notes.firstAction: Note the start/end time of the latest scan rather than interpreting every old log entry.
steps: Open the current CBS log through Microsoft’s documented SFC detail workflow and inspect entries marked [SR] for that run.
Record the unresolved component names and servicing errors privately; distinguish old repaired entries from current failures.
Use the matching supported servicing or repair-install route, then rerun the relevant verification and the original failing feature.
notes.expected: The case identifies the current unresolved component or records a clean final scan and working feature.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not take ownership of protected files or copy binaries from another random PC as a generic repair.

notes.title: Repair one broken app without resetting the PC
notes.symptom: Windows works normally but one installed application will not open or behaves incorrectly.
notes.firstAction: Confirm that the same failure is limited to that application and protect its local-only data.
steps: Open Settings > Apps > Installed apps, choose the affected app’s menu and open Advanced options if available.
Use Repair first when offered, then retest. Review the displayed data effects before considering Reset; reset can remove local app state.
For desktop programs without that option, use the publisher-supported Modify/Repair path in Programs and Features or its installer.
notes.expected: The original application task works with the required data, settings and account access verified.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the fault affects several Windows components or data cannot be protected, use the system or application-owner route before resetting.

notes.title: Clear an update’s storage blocker safely
notes.symptom: Windows Update asks for more space or fails during a low-space installation.
notes.firstAction: Open Settings > System > Storage and record available space before deleting anything.
steps: Review the supported temporary-file and cleanup choices; keep Downloads, customer files and rollback material unless their removal is explicitly intended.
If the update offers external storage, follow that specific workflow using a trusted device and keep it attached for the required phase.
Retry the same update, restart when requested and confirm its entry in Update history.
notes.expected: The identified update completes and the user’s data and rollback decision remain accounted for.
notes.ifUnresolved: If space rapidly disappears again, identify the owning files or service; do not repeatedly erase logs needed to diagnose the failure.

notes.title: Find why a feature upgrade rolled back
notes.symptom: Windows returns to the previous version after an attempted feature upgrade.
notes.firstAction: Preserve the failed-upgrade logs before cleanup or another installation attempt.
steps: Use the current official SetupDiag workflow to analyze the applicable setup logs and retain its result file.
Read the matched failure rule, phase and operation alongside the original logs; separate the last failure from earlier warnings.
Correct the specific driver, application or servicing blocker identified by the evidence, then plan one controlled retry.
notes.expected: The retry targets a documented blocker and either succeeds or produces a distinct new failure record.
notes.ifUnresolved: SetupDiag is an analyzer, not an automatic repair. Escalate unmatched or contradictory results with the preserved logs.

notes.title: Check why a feature update is not offered
notes.symptom: A device receives routine updates but a newer feature release is missing.
notes.firstAction: Record the installed edition/build and whether update settings are organization-managed.
steps: Compare the target release with the official release-health page and the device’s hardware/application compatibility issue.
Ask the update owner to check deployment policy and safeguard status; distinguish a deliberate ring delay from a compatibility hold.
Apply the documented prerequisite or wait for the resolved issue, then recheck the offer through the approved update path.
notes.expected: The missing offer has an explicit policy or compatibility explanation and an approved next step.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not bypass a safeguard or force installation solely because another PC received the update.

notes.title: Find a disk missing from recovery media
notes.symptom: Firmware sees the disk but Windows installation or recovery media does not.
notes.firstAction: Confirm the disk is consistently detected in firmware and identify the exact storage controller/model.
steps: Obtain the model-specific storage-controller driver for the recovery environment’s architecture from the OEM.
Use the supported Load driver option in Windows Setup where applicable, then inspect the disk list again.
Keep the original storage-controller mode documented; do not change RAID/VMD/AHCI settings as an unexplained workaround.
notes.expected: The correct disk and existing partitions appear without initializing, formatting or altering the storage mode.
notes.ifUnresolved: If firmware detection is unstable or the OEM driver does not expose the disk, move to hardware/data recovery before write operations.

notes.title: Identify the Windows volume inside recovery
notes.symptom: An offline repair cannot find Windows or appears to target the wrong drive.
notes.firstAction: Treat drive letters in the recovery environment as unverified until the actual volumes are identified.
steps: In the recovery Command Prompt, run diskpart, then list volume, then exit; compare volume sizes and labels without formatting or modifying partitions, and verify the candidate volume’s encryption state.
Inspect the candidate volume for the expected Windows and user folders; unlock the intended encrypted volume through its approved recovery key if required.
Use that verified volume only in the product’s documented offline repair syntax and retain the target identity in the private ticket.
notes.expected: The offline operation addresses the intended installation, not the USB, recovery partition or another attached disk.
notes.ifUnresolved: Stop if the target cannot be distinguished or the source is failing; never assume that C: identifies the installed OS in recovery.

notes.title: Find the matching BitLocker key
notes.symptom: A stored recovery key is rejected or several similarly named device records exist.
notes.firstAction: Read the recovery-key ID displayed by the affected device.
steps: Use a separate trusted device to open the approved personal or organization recovery store and match the key ID, not just the computer name.
Check the account that originally enabled encryption or the organization’s administrator-held record when the expected account has no match.
Enter the matching recovery key locally and verify the intended volume unlocks; record only the approved private reference in the service ticket.
notes.expected: The encrypted installation unlocks with the record matching its displayed key ID.
notes.ifUnresolved: If no valid key is available, stop data-destructive reset/reinstall decisions until the owner understands the recovery limit.

notes.title: Try filesystem undelete before file carving
notes.symptom: Files were deleted from a healthy NTFS volume and original names or folders matter.
notes.firstAction: Stop writes to the affected filesystem and prepare a separate destination.
steps: On a healthy source or preserved working image, use TestDisk’s documented Advanced > partition > Undelete path for NTFS.
Select the recoverable files and copy them to the separate destination; do not write partition-table changes merely to undelete files.
Open representative results. Use PhotoRec as the fallback when filesystem metadata no longer supplies the needed files.
notes.expected: Recovered files are usable, with original metadata retained where the filesystem still provides it.
notes.ifUnresolved: If media is unstable, return to imaging first. No undelete method can promise data already overwritten or discarded.

notes.title: Resume imaging without swapping source and target
notes.symptom: A recovery session stopped and device names changed after reconnecting or rebooting.
notes.firstAction: Match the source and destination by model, serial and size before resuming anything.
steps: Locate the existing image and persistent mapfile on healthy storage and confirm they belong to this acquisition.
Re-read the intended input/output paths and the ddrescue command against the acquisition record; never rely on the old letter or device order alone.
Resume with the matching mapfile under the documented recovery policy, retaining earlier checkpoints and stopping if the source deteriorates.
notes.expected: The operation continues the same acquisition and its mapfile records exactly which ranges remain incomplete.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not resume if device identity, mapfile pairing or destination overwrite scope cannot be proved.

notes.title: Validate carved files without trusting their filenames
notes.symptom: PhotoRec produces numbered folders and files rather than the original directory tree.
notes.firstAction: Treat recovered names and extensions as output labels, then test the contents.
steps: Use PhotoRec’s documented file-type selection for the formats needed and send output to separate healthy storage.
Open representative documents, images and archives with their real applications; check complete contents rather than only thumbnails or file size.
Record missing filenames/folders, failed samples and any priority application validation; keep the source/image until acceptance.
notes.expected: The report distinguishes usable recovered content from the original metadata that carving did not restore.
notes.ifUnresolved: If encrypted or fragmented priority files remain unusable, stop treating a large output count as successful recovery and escalate that specific format.

notes.title: Use remaining space after a successful clone
notes.symptom: A larger replacement disk boots correctly but the Windows volume is still the old size.
notes.firstAction: Open Disk Management and inspect the partition order on the verified new disk.
steps: Confirm unallocated space exists on that same disk and whether it is immediately after the volume to extend.
Use Extend Volume only when the documented filesystem/layout requirements are met and a rollback copy exists.
Reopen the volume and verify capacity, applications and recovery behavior before releasing the original disk.
notes.expected: The intended volume uses the approved additional space and the migrated system still boots independently.
notes.ifUnresolved: If a recovery or other partition blocks extension, plan a supported layout change; do not delete partitions just to make the option clickable.

notes.title: Read a copy result correctly
notes.symptom: A Robocopy job reports a nonzero exit code and a wrapper labels the whole migration failed.
notes.firstAction: Retain the copy log and the exact exit code before rerunning.
steps: Compare the result with Microsoft’s return-code table: codes below 8 describe successful copies or differences; 8 or higher includes a failure.
Review copied, skipped, extra, mismatch and failed totals against the intended scope rather than accepting only the headline code.
Open representative destination files as the intended user and investigate any failed or mismatched items individually.
notes.expected: The case identifies actual copy failures or documented differences and verifies usable destination data.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not add mirror or purge flags to make the totals match; those can delete destination files.

notes.title: Finish what an app-list import cannot migrate
notes.symptom: Applications reinstall on the new PC but settings, licenses or data are missing.
notes.firstAction: Separate the application inventory from the user-data and license migration records.
steps: Review WinGet export/import results for packages that were unmatched, unavailable or installed from a different source.
Install missing approved products from their publisher and restore settings/data through each application’s supported method.
Activate the correct licenses and test a real user document or workflow for each critical application.
notes.expected: The migration proves working applications and user data rather than merely reproducing a package list.
notes.ifUnresolved: Keep the old device or rollback copy until unique local data and licensed application access are accounted for.

notes.title: Include cloud-only files in the recovery plan
notes.symptom: A local backup or migrated folder contains OneDrive placeholders instead of usable offline files.
notes.firstAction: Inspect the affected files’ OneDrive status icons and confirm the intended account.
steps: For files that must be available locally, choose Always keep on this device and wait for the download to finish with enough disk space.
Open representative files while disconnected from the network to prove local availability before relying on a filesystem copy.
Run the approved backup, restore those samples to a separate destination and test them there.
notes.expected: The restore contains real usable content, not only cloud references that still depend on the original account.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the cloud account, retention or download is blocked, record that recovery gap rather than marking the local backup complete.

notes.title: Check repository data as well as metadata
notes.symptom: A restic repository check passes but no restored file has been tested.
notes.firstAction: Record the snapshot ID and the scope of the check that actually ran.
steps: Distinguish restic check’s structural checks from the documented read-data options that read stored data packs.
Choose an authorized data-verification scope appropriate to repository size, connection cost and the service window.
Restore representative priority files from the selected snapshot to a separate target and open them with their real applications.
notes.expected: The record states which data was read and which restored files were usable, with sample limits explicit.
notes.ifUnresolved: A metadata-only pass cannot establish every file’s recoverability; investigate reported pack errors without pruning the only repository copy.

notes.title: Recover an older version without overwriting current work
notes.symptom: The owner needs an earlier file version but current edits must be retained.
notes.firstAction: Confirm the required recovery date and create a separate restore destination.
steps: Select the correct source device and recovery point in the matching backup product.
Use its copy-to-new-location or alternate-destination restore choice instead of restoring over the live file.
Open both versions with the owner, verify permissions and decide which approved version should become active.
notes.expected: The requested earlier content is recovered while the current working copy remains available.
notes.ifUnresolved: If an application database requires its own restore process, use that workflow on a safe copy rather than copying open database files blindly.

notes.title: Prove the backup can be opened after the PC is lost
notes.symptom: Backups run automatically, but only the original machine appears to know the repository password.
notes.firstAction: Identify the approved credential/recovery store without copying secrets into the public record.
steps: From a separate trusted restore environment, follow the product’s existing-repository connection procedure with the authorized credentials.
List the expected snapshots and restore a harmless representative file to a separate location.
Record the private credential reference, required software and tested restore route so another authorized technician can repeat it.
notes.expected: Recovery succeeds without relying on the original workstation’s saved session or local configuration.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the encryption password or recovery material is unavailable, preserve the repository and escalate; do not create a new repository over it.

notes.title: Fix a PC stuck on a self-assigned address
notes.symptom: A DHCP-configured adapter has a 169.254 address and cannot reach the normal gateway.
notes.firstAction: Run ipconfig /all and identify the affected adapter, DHCP state and lease information.
steps: Check the actual cable/Wi-Fi association and compare one working device on the same intended network.
Inspect the DHCP Client service and its Admin/Operational event logs; distinguish one-PC failure from a VLAN, scope or server problem.
Restore the proven DHCP path, then renew only the affected adapter when a local or alternate access path is available.
notes.expected: The adapter receives the intended lease, gateway and DNS settings and reaches the required service.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not invent a static address or release the adapter carrying the only remote session. Escalate shared lease failures to the network owner.

notes.title: Restore internal name resolution on VPN
notes.symptom: Public websites work, but a company share or application name fails after VPN connection.
notes.firstAction: Compare the failing full hostname and DNS settings with a working approved client.
steps: Run Resolve-DnsName for the actual service name and note the answer or error and the configured resolver.
Check whether the approved VPN installed the intended DNS server, suffix and route to that server; distinguish a short-name problem from a full-name problem.
Correct the managed DNS/VPN setting through its owner and retest the original application, not only a DNS query.
notes.expected: The intended internal name resolves through the correct path and the user can access the service.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not replace domain DNS with a public resolver or weaken the firewall to hide a missing route.

notes.title: Complete a captive Wi-Fi sign-in
notes.symptom: The PC associates with guest Wi-Fi but internet access is limited until the network’s sign-in step.
notes.firstAction: Confirm the exact network name with the venue or network owner.
steps: Use the operating system’s network sign-in notification or the owner’s documented portal page and inspect the destination before entering information.
Complete the approved access terms or account step; do not dismiss a certificate warning or enter organization credentials into an unexpected page.
Recheck ordinary browsing and the required VPN/application after the portal releases access.
notes.expected: The portal state completes and an ordinary secure site plus the intended service works.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the portal loops or the network identity is uncertain, involve the network owner; avoid broad proxy/VPN/security changes just to expose a page.

notes.title: Separate a blocked port from a DNS problem
notes.symptom: The expected hostname resolves, but one application cannot connect.
notes.firstAction: Identify the application’s documented destination and TCP port.
steps: Run Test-NetConnection with the actual ComputerName and Port values; record the chosen interface and TcpTestSucceeded result.
Compare the same test from an approved working client and the intended VPN/proxy state.
If TCP succeeds, test authentication, certificates and the application itself; if it fails, have the network/service owner inspect that specific path.
notes.expected: The evidence isolates transport reachability from application behavior without changing unrelated network settings.
notes.ifUnresolved: A successful ping does not prove the service port works, and a successful TCP handshake does not prove the application is healthy.

notes.title: Locate a throughput bottleneck
notes.symptom: Large transfers are slow, but browsing and connectivity checks pass.
notes.firstAction: Choose approved test endpoints and compare the same transfer over wired and wireless paths.
steps: Check the negotiated link and use a known-good cable/port when the observed link is below the device’s expected capability.
For a controlled LAN test, use iperf3 on an upstream-supported Linux/macOS/FreeBSD endpoint pair with the server restricted to the approved test network.
Compare LAN results with the real file/application transfer before blaming the internet connection, storage or Wi-Fi.
notes.expected: Like-for-like measurements show which path or endpoint introduces the bottleneck.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not advertise an unverified third-party Windows build as upstream iperf3 or run an unrestricted public test server.

notes.title: Read an unexpected-restart event correctly
notes.symptom: Event 41 appears after a power outage or unexplained restart.
notes.firstAction: Match the event time with the actual outage and user report.
steps: Inspect the event’s bug-check information and nearby system events; Event 41 records an unclean shutdown, not a single proven cause.
Check power/UPS and hardware evidence when there is no useful bug check; follow the crash-dump route when a stop code and dump exist.
After the scoped correction, observe a normal shutdown/startup and the affected business service.
notes.expected: The case distinguishes a recorded unclean shutdown from evidence for power, hardware or software cause.
notes.ifUnresolved: Stop repeated power cycling when storage, electrical safety or thermal symptoms appear.

notes.title: Recover a dependent service in the right order
notes.symptom: The server is running after power restoration but one business service remains unavailable.
notes.firstAction: Identify the exact service name and its required dependencies before restarting anything.
steps: Open Services or use the read-only Get-Service view to inspect state and required/dependent services.
Review service-start events and verify storage, DNS, identity and any database dependency before the approved start/restart.
Test the real user operation from a client and retain the service error if it stops again.
notes.expected: The service stays running because its dependencies work, and the business transaction succeeds.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not mass-start or repeatedly restart every service. Recurring termination needs the application or infrastructure owner.

notes.title: Restore a share after the server returns
notes.symptom: The server responds, but a previously working file share or mapped drive does not.
notes.firstAction: Test the approved share by its normal hostname from an affected user session.
steps: Separate name resolution, the required SMB connection and authentication; compare with a working client and the server’s service state.
Check whether the backing volume and intended share are available and whether the original permissions remain intact.
Repair the proven dependency, then open and save an agreed test file as the actual user.
notes.expected: The normal share path works with the intended permissions and data, not only with an administrator account.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not expose the share broadly or enable obsolete SMB versions as a generic outage workaround.

notes.title: Move a required file through an approved route
notes.symptom: Screen control works, but the required installer or diagnostic file cannot be transferred.
notes.firstAction: Confirm the exact file, transfer direction and approved destination with the user.
steps: For an installer, open the verified publisher link on the target PC where possible instead of assuming clipboard copy is file transfer.
For private evidence, verify the chosen client’s file-transfer capability and permission or use the approved private transfer service.
Check the received file’s identity and readable content, then apply the agreed retention/removal decision.
notes.expected: The intended file reaches the correct private destination without copying unrelated customer data.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the selected session lacks the necessary capability, change to an approved route; do not deploy an unplanned unattended agent.

notes.title: Restore Mac screen sharing and control
notes.symptom: A RustDesk session connects to a Mac but the screen is blank or input does not work.
notes.firstAction: Have the authorized local user inspect the permissions on the controlled Mac.
steps: Follow the current RustDesk macOS installation guidance, including the intended Applications location and helper installation where required.
Grant the required Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions in System Settings > Privacy & Security; apply any documented Input Monitoring requirement for that setup.
Restart the app/session when prompted and test screen visibility and one harmless control action.
notes.expected: The correct screen is visible and the authorized control action works with the user’s consent.
notes.ifUnresolved: If local approval is unavailable or management policy blocks the permission, arrange an approved local/managed-support path instead of bypassing it.

notes.title: Avoid losing the session during a restart
notes.symptom: The next repair requires rebooting, changing the network adapter or restarting security software.
notes.firstAction: Agree how the user and technician will reconnect before making the change.
steps: For an attended code-based session, keep the user available to reopen the app and approve a new connection when needed.
For existing managed access, verify the assigned device, service startup and approved reconnect behavior before restarting.
After reconnecting, confirm the same machine and user context and retest the original repair outcome.
notes.expected: The session resumes through the agreed route without creating unplanned permanent access.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the only connection would be lost and no local person or recovery channel exists, defer the disruptive action.

notes.title: Fix domain discovery before changing trust
notes.symptom: The member PC reports a trust/sign-in fault while internal domain names also fail.
notes.firstAction: Read the member’s active IP and DNS configuration on the intended network or VPN.
steps: Compare the DNS servers and suffix with a working domain client, then resolve the actual domain/service names through the approved resolver.
Restore the managed DNS/VPN route before running a secure-channel diagnostic.
Use Windows PowerShell 5.1 to repeat the member-only Test-ComputerSecureChannel check and test a normal sign-in.
notes.expected: Domain discovery works and the trust test now gives a meaningful result over a working network path.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not rejoin the domain or point the member at public DNS to work around missing domain connectivity.

notes.title: Restore the domain time path
notes.symptom: Domain authentication fails and the member clock differs materially from the domain’s reference.
notes.firstAction: Read the current clock and w32tm /query /status without changing time providers.
steps: Check the reported time source and whether the member can reach the intended domain synchronization path.
Have the domain owner correct the configuration or connectivity under the organization’s policy, preserving evidence of the old state.
After synchronization, retry domain authentication and the required share/application.
notes.expected: The member follows the approved time hierarchy and authentication succeeds without bypassing policy.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not apply a generic public-NTP recipe to domain controllers or all members; wider clock failure belongs to the directory owner.

notes.title: Check computer identity after restoring an old image
notes.symptom: Trust broke after cloning, renaming or restoring a domain-joined workstation.
notes.firstAction: Record the restoration time and whether another active PC uses the same computer identity.
steps: Have the directory administrator compare the intended computer object, recent resets and duplicate-machine evidence.
Keep a working local recovery account and correct the identity conflict before a scoped member secure-channel repair.
Restart as planned, test a fresh domain sign-in and verify group policy, shares and business apps.
notes.expected: One intended machine owns the correct computer identity and its secure channel remains healthy.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not repeatedly reset or delete the computer object while two active machines compete for it; do not use this member procedure on a domain controller.

notes.title: Bring classic Outlook back online
notes.symptom: Messages stay in Outbox and the classic client shows Working Offline.
notes.firstAction: Check the status bar and whether Send/Receive > Work Offline is highlighted.
steps: Select Work Offline to return online, then confirm the status changes rather than repeatedly clicking without observing it.
Send/receive again and compare the account in webmail if the client still shows Disconnected.
Verify one agreed test message is sent and received and that queued mail is reconciled.
notes.expected: The client shows a connected state and messages leave the Outbox normally.
notes.ifUnresolved: If webmail also fails or the client is new Outlook, use the appropriate account/service or new-client route instead of classic-only controls.

notes.title: Release a message stuck behind a large attachment
notes.symptom: One classic Outlook message remains in Outbox while sending is stalled.
notes.firstAction: Confirm the recipient and preserve the message text before changing the stuck item.
steps: Switch classic Outlook to Work Offline and move the affected message to Drafts using Microsoft’s documented procedure.
Remove the oversized attachment and use an approved sharing link or a smaller permitted file; preserve unrelated queued messages.
Return online, send the corrected message and verify delivery through the normal account path.
notes.expected: The corrected message leaves Outbox and the remaining queue resumes without duplicate or unintended sends.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the message remains locked, close/reopen the client as documented; do not delete the whole profile or mailbox to clear one item.

notes.title: Move an active PST out of the sync bottleneck
notes.symptom: OneDrive stays on Processing changes or reports a file in use while Outlook uses a PST in the sync folder.
notes.firstAction: Identify the exact PST and protect a closed, usable backup before moving it.
steps: Close Outlook and follow Microsoft’s PST relocation procedure to a suitable local location outside the active OneDrive sync path.
Reconnect the data file through Outlook’s supported data-file controls and verify its folders and representative mail.
Resume normal OneDrive activity and configure a separate approved backup for the local mail file.
notes.expected: Outlook opens the intended mail data and the sync queue clears without treating synchronization as the only PST backup.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the PST contains unique mail or is damaged, preserve the original and use the data-file recovery path before further movement.

notes.title: Find mail missing only from the local cache
notes.symptom: Older mail appears in webmail but is absent or unavailable offline in classic Outlook.
notes.firstAction: Confirm the same mailbox and folder in webmail before treating the messages as deleted.
steps: In classic Outlook inspect File > Account Settings > Account Settings, select the Exchange/Microsoft 365 account and check the offline-mail synchronization range.
Choose the approved range for the device and available storage, then allow synchronization to complete.
Search the same known older message and test offline access if that is required for the user’s work.
notes.expected: The case distinguishes server-held mail from locally cached mail and proves the intended access mode.
notes.ifUnresolved: If messages are missing from the server too, investigate retention, archive, deletion or permissions rather than rebuilding the cache.

notes.title: Match a stale printer port to the current device
notes.symptom: A network printer went offline after a router change, lease change or network move.
notes.firstAction: Print the printer’s own network report and match its model/MAC to the intended device.
steps: Read the selected queue’s PortName with Get-Printer and inspect that port with Get-PrinterPort in Windows PowerShell 5.1.
Compare the current device address with the configured TCP/IP port; use the supported queue/port settings to correct only the proven mismatch.
Test the Windows page and original document, then coordinate any reservation or managed-address correction with the network owner.
notes.expected: The intended queue reaches the correct physical device and keeps its trays, duplex and other required options.
notes.ifUnresolved: WSD, shared-server and USB queues use different bindings. Do not rewrite all ports or assign an arbitrary static address.

notes.title: Resolve an incompatible printer-driver package
notes.symptom: A vendor installer is rejected on an ARM PC or a protected-print device.
notes.firstAction: Check Settings > System > About and the active Windows protected print mode policy.
steps: If protected print mode applies, choose the supported IPP/Mopria path and the appropriate Print Support App rather than forcing a legacy third-party driver.
If a conventional package is appropriate, use the exact OEM model page and match Windows version plus native architecture.
Verify a real document and required device options before removing the old working queue.
notes.expected: The selected print path is supported by the device architecture and active security mode.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the printer depends on an unsupported driver, involve the managed print owner; do not casually disable protected print mode.

notes.title: Fix streaks that occur only through the feeder
notes.symptom: Scans or copies show a vertical line from the ADF, while a flatbed copy is clean.
notes.firstAction: Copy the same clean original once from the flatbed and once from the feeder, marking which is which.
steps: Use the exact model’s cleaning instructions to locate its narrow ADF glass strip and backing surface.
Power down or disconnect as the manufacturer instructs and clean only the specified surfaces with the approved method; do not spray liquid into the unit.
Repeat the paired flatbed/ADF test and save a sample of the corrected multipage output.
notes.expected: The feeder-specific line disappears while the flatbed and normal printing remain correct.
notes.ifUnresolved: Persistent lines on both paths or damaged glass need the model’s service procedure, not another Windows driver installation.

notes.title: Make the scanner appear in the scan profile
notes.symptom: Printing works, but the scan application cannot find the multifunction device.
notes.firstAction: Confirm the scanner’s connection and the actual OS architecture independently of the print queue.
steps: In NAPS2 choose New Profile > Choose device and inspect the supported WIA, TWAIN and eSCL choices.
Use the correct manufacturer scan driver for WIA/TWAIN, or eSCL for a compatible network scanner; do not assume a working print driver supplies scanning.
Scan and save one page, then test the required ADF/duplex workflow and open the saved PDF.
notes.expected: The intended scanner is selectable and the saved file contains every requested page in order.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the device is not supported through the chosen protocol or policy blocks discovery, use the exact OEM scan path or managed network owner.

notes.title: Separate a bad document from a broken printer
notes.symptom: A single PDF fails, but the printer’s internal page and other documents print.
notes.firstAction: Keep the original file and test a simple one-page document on the same queue.
steps: Open the PDF in SumatraPDF and use Ctrl+P to try a single page with the same paper size and queue.
Compare page rendering and the exact print error; check whether only particular pages, fonts or embedded content trigger it.
Use the document/viewer’s supported correction or obtain a clean source copy, then print the required pages and confirm layout.
notes.expected: The test identifies a document/viewer-specific failure without changing every user’s driver or spooler.
notes.ifUnresolved: If all applications fail, return to the queue/device branch. Preserve confidential document contents when escalating to the author.

notes.title: Capture usable evidence for the next crash
notes.symptom: A real stop error occurs but no usable memory dump is available.
notes.firstAction: Check the configured dump type, target path, free space and page-file state.
steps: Open System Properties > Advanced > Startup and Recovery and select the organization’s appropriate supported dump setting.
Confirm that the page file or dedicated dump file meets the selected dump’s requirements; a disabled or undersized page file can prevent capture.
After the next naturally occurring crash, preserve the resulting dump privately and analyze it with the crash time and recent changes.
notes.expected: A usable dump and matching event evidence are available for the specific crash.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not force a production crash just to test logging without a separate authorized plan; dumps can contain customer data.

notes.title: Isolate a memory fault after an upgrade
notes.symptom: Crashes or memory-test errors began after changing RAM or firmware memory settings.
notes.firstAction: Record the installed modules, slots and current firmware settings before opening the device.
steps: Check the exact motherboard/device memory requirements and restore an approved supported configuration before comparing results.
Boot Memtest86+ through a supported, approved firmware path and record which test/configuration produces errors.
Following the hardware service procedure, compare modules and slots individually to distinguish a module, slot or configuration problem.
notes.expected: Errors are reproducible in a documented configuration or the corrected supported configuration completes the planned test.
notes.ifUnresolved: A passing sample does not exclude every intermittent fault; stop if disassembly, firmware security or unsupported hardware exceeds the service scope.

notes.title: Find a device failing through a USB hub
notes.symptom: A scanner, printer or storage device disconnects through a dock but works intermittently elsewhere.
notes.firstAction: Record the device, hub/dock, cable and physical port used for the failure.
steps: Compare the same device on a known-good direct port and cable without moving unrelated production devices.
Use USB Device Tree Viewer to identify the actual hub chain and negotiated connection, then check the dock/device’s power and firmware requirements.
Apply the evidenced cable, port, power or supported firmware correction and repeat a sustained real transfer or scan.
notes.expected: The original workload remains connected on the documented path, with the failed component or topology isolated.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not use a failing storage device for repeated transfer stress; preserve its data first.

notes.title: Restore network access during device setup
notes.symptom: A newly installed PC has no working network adapter during Windows setup.
notes.firstAction: Identify the exact device model and architecture from the hardware record.
steps: Check the physical connection and try an approved supported Ethernet path if available.
From a trusted working PC, obtain the exact OEM network driver and follow Microsoft’s documented setup-time driver installation route.
Complete the intended organization enrollment after connectivity returns and verify the adapter in Device Manager.
notes.expected: The PC reaches the intended setup/enrollment service through a supported network adapter.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not use account-bypass scripts or random driver bundles to conceal an unresolved network or enrollment problem.

notes.title: Make the package manager available to the user
notes.symptom: The winget command is not recognized on a newly prepared supported Windows PC.
notes.firstAction: Check the supported Windows version, current user sign-in and App Installer availability.
steps: Use Microsoft’s documented Windows Package Manager installation/registration path; on supported desktop Windows it is supplied through App Installer.
Update or repair the approved App Installer deployment through its supported source and open a fresh user terminal.
Run winget --info, then inspect one approved package before starting the workstation’s application install list.
notes.expected: The actual user can invoke WinGet and its configured sources are the intended ones.
notes.ifUnresolved: If store access is managed or the platform is unsupported, use the organization’s deployment route instead of downloading a random replacement executable.

notes.title: Confirm the intended organization device state
notes.symptom: A work account is present, but the device does not receive expected management or sign-in behavior.
notes.firstAction: Compare the intended enrollment/join design with Settings > Accounts > Access work or school.
steps: Distinguish adding an account to an app, registering a device and joining it to the organization’s directory.
Have the device-management owner verify the device record and required enrollment path before disconnecting or rejoining anything.
After the supported correction, test the intended user sign-in, policy delivery and required managed application.
notes.expected: The device has the expected identity and management state, with a real policy/application result.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not remove the only working account or destroy the user profile to force a different enrollment state.

notes.title: Prove the repair under the real user account
notes.symptom: The technician can open a repaired or restored file, but the normal user gets Access denied.
notes.firstAction: Reproduce the exact task under the intended standard-user account.
steps: Compare the intended path and file ownership/permissions with a working equivalent; use a read-only permissions view before changing ACLs.
Correct only the identified ownership or access issue through the approved application/share/file owner.
Have the user reopen, edit and save an agreed test item without elevation.
notes.expected: The user’s actual workflow succeeds with the intended limited permissions.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not grant Everyone full control or make the user an administrator to hide a permission fault.

notes.title: Make recovery information retrievable
notes.symptom: Encryption works, but the owner cannot locate the recovery record during handoff.
notes.firstAction: Identify the approved account or organization store that should hold the recovery key.
steps: Use a separate trusted device to verify that the authorized owner can reach the relevant recovery record and match the device/key identity.
If the key is not backed up, follow the supported key-backup procedure using the approved destination.
Record the private retrieval reference and responsible owner without copying the secret into the public wiki or ordinary handoff text.
notes.expected: The authorized owner can retrieve the correct recovery material independently of the repaired PC.
notes.ifUnresolved: If retrieval cannot be demonstrated, leave that recovery gap explicitly open rather than claiming the machine is fully recoverable.

notes.title: Remove access that was only for this repair
notes.symptom: A temporary support program or unattended setting still starts after the case ends.
notes.firstAction: Compare the current installation/access state with the agreed end state for this device.
steps: End all case-only sessions and remove the temporary unattended credential or enrollment through that product’s supported controls.
Uninstall a case-only client when appropriate; keep the organization’s approved persistent management agent intact.
Restart if required and verify that the temporary access is gone while approved support and the repaired task still work.
notes.expected: Remaining access has an explicit owner and purpose; one-case access no longer functions.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the temporary and managed deployments cannot be distinguished, involve the management owner before removing agents or services.

notes.title: Resolve a Secure Boot rejection deliberately
notes.symptom: A prepared rescue USB is detected but its bootloader is rejected by Secure Boot.
notes.firstAction: Record the exact firmware message and verify the USB image/publisher before changing firmware settings.
steps: Check the tool’s documented Secure Boot support and the device’s approved firmware policy.
If using Ventoy, follow its current supported enrollment or compatibility procedure only with the owner’s authorization and verified files.
Boot-test the intended image and record the final security state along with storage/network access.
notes.expected: The approved recovery environment boots through the documented trust path and required security settings are accounted for.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not enroll an unverified key or disable Secure Boot as a universal troubleshooting step.

notes.title: Choose media that can boot the target
notes.symptom: A rescue image works on an x64 PC but not on an ARM device.
notes.firstAction: Check the target’s actual architecture before rewriting the same USB again.
steps: Choose the official image and boot tool that explicitly support the target architecture and firmware mode.
For Windows ARM recovery, follow Microsoft’s ARM64 media requirements and obtain required model-specific drivers.
Boot-test on the intended class of device and verify its storage and input devices before putting the USB into service.
notes.expected: The recovery environment actually starts on the target architecture and can access the required hardware.
notes.ifUnresolved: An amd64/x64 rescue ISO is not universal ARM recovery media; use the device’s supported recovery route when an image is unavailable.

notes.title: Handle an image larger than the USB filesystem limit
notes.symptom: Copying a large ISO or installation file fails even though the USB has enough total free space.
notes.firstAction: Check the USB filesystem and the exact file size before deleting files or changing partitions.
steps: Distinguish a filesystem’s single-file limit from total capacity; use the media tool’s documented layout rather than manually forcing a random format.
For a supported multiboot workflow, use Ventoy’s documented data-partition filesystem support; for a single image, let Rufus prepare the supported boot layout.
Verify the written/copied image and boot-test it in the intended UEFI/Secure Boot configuration.
notes.expected: The complete image fits and boots on the intended machine, not merely on the preparation PC.
notes.ifUnresolved: Formatting or installing the boot manager can erase the USB; stop if the target device or retained files are uncertain.

notes.title: Create a safe diagnostic excerpt
notes.symptom: A log or screenshot contains customer names, addresses, tokens or recovery information.
notes.firstAction: Prepare a local copy and keep the original evidence in the approved private case record.
steps: Extract only the error, relevant timestamps and nonsecret configuration needed for the question; replace identifiers consistently so relationships remain understandable.
Review the excerpt for credentials, authorization headers, private paths and embedded file contents before sending it to an approved AI service.
Check the applicable workspace data controls and retain a private mapping only when the case needs it.
notes.expected: The shared excerpt still supports diagnosis without exposing the original customer identity or secrets.
notes.ifUnresolved: If useful analysis requires restricted raw data, use an approved environment or specialist instead of assuming a privacy toggle makes disclosure acceptable.

notes.title: Check a suggested command before running it
notes.symptom: An AI answer supplies a command for a different shell, OS version or target.
notes.firstAction: Identify the actual shell/version and whether the command reads or changes state.
steps: Use the exact publisher documentation and a read-only Get-Command/Get-Help check where appropriate to confirm the command and supported parameters.
Replace illustrative placeholders only after identifying the real target, privileges and rollback; do not paste an entire mixed command block.
Run the smallest approved diagnostic first and compare the output with the answer’s predicted result.
notes.expected: The command is valid for the actual environment and its observed result supports the next action.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the tool is missing or the proposal includes unexplained destructive flags, stop and revise the plan rather than bypassing execution controls.

notes.title: Keep a log or webpage from changing the task
notes.symptom: Retrieved content tells the assistant to ignore instructions, reveal secrets or run unrelated commands.
notes.firstAction: Treat that text as untrusted evidence rather than authorization.
steps: State the diagnostic question and allowed data/action scope separately from the quoted log or webpage.
Keep code-agent filesystem, network and approval controls appropriate to the task; inspect proposed tool calls and diffs before granting broader access.
Verify the factual claim against a primary source and continue only the repair action supported by the actual user request.
notes.expected: The investigation uses relevant evidence without following embedded instructions or exposing unrelated data.
notes.ifUnresolved: If the task cannot proceed within approved controls, preserve the finding and escalate the access requirement rather than weakening the boundary.

notes.title: Use the supported optimization for the drive type
notes.symptom: A maintenance request proposes repeatedly defragmenting or cleaning every drive.
notes.firstAction: Check drive health and open Defragment and Optimize Drives to identify the media type and current status.
steps: Use Windows’ supported optimization for that media and review the scheduled state rather than applying an HDD-style routine to every device.
Investigate low free space or real I/O faults separately; optimization is not a repair for a failing drive.
Retest the user’s workload and retain the observed health/performance result.
notes.expected: The appropriate maintenance completes without disguising an unresolved storage fault.
notes.ifUnresolved: Stop write-heavy maintenance if the disk disconnects, reports I/O errors or contains the only unprotected data copy.

notes.title: Update an app missing from the package-manager list
notes.symptom: An installed program is outdated but does not appear as a normal WinGet upgrade.
notes.firstAction: Identify the publisher, installed version and how the application was originally deployed.
steps: Inspect the package match and configured source; distinguish an unknown version, pinned package or unmanaged installer from a fully current app.
Use the approved exact package or publisher update mechanism and respect organization deployment policy.
Launch the app, check the resulting version and test its important file/workflow before considering the update complete.
notes.expected: The identified application is updated through its intended source and still works for the user.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not force every unknown package or bypass a pin without understanding the compatibility or management reason.

notes.title: Resume a stalled cloud-sync workflow
notes.symptom: New files remain on one PC and the OneDrive icon shows paused or an error state.
notes.firstAction: Open the sync client’s activity/status view and identify the actual pause or error.
steps: Resume synchronization through the supported control when it is simply paused; for errors, resolve the named account, storage, filename or connectivity issue.
Wait for the relevant file’s completed state and verify the expected version through the intended cloud account or another authorized device.
Keep backup/retention checks separate because synchronization can propagate deletion or unwanted changes.
notes.expected: The expected file version reaches the intended account and the client no longer reports an unresolved sync state.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not unlink, reset or delete the local folder before accounting for unsynced local-only files.

notes.title: Find an operating system outside its support plan
notes.symptom: The device is usable but its installed Windows release may no longer receive the required updates.
notes.firstAction: Record the exact edition, version and build from Settings > System > About.
steps: Check the current official lifecycle/release-health information for that release and the organization’s recorded servicing or ESU entitlement.
Separate missing monthly updates from an unsupported feature release or an absent extended-security plan.
Document the approved upgrade/replacement route, application compatibility checks and backup/rollback requirements.
notes.expected: The maintenance record states the real support position and a concrete owner/date for any needed transition.
notes.ifUnresolved: Do not label every older installation safe merely because Windows Update says no updates are available.
